READABILITY.evidence: Names say what they do (durabilityTracker, statusLocked, recordJobLocked, durabilityWaiterHeap). Every public type and method has a doc comment, and the non-obvious parts are explained, e.g. 'The WAL is written sequentially, so a successful sync…'. Single letters are only idiomatic Go receivers.

MAINTAINABILITY.evidence: The dedicated tracker in durability.go (487 lines) is well structured. But the long d.batchDurable(seqNum,count,size,correlationID,applyDuration,walWritten.Elapsed(),err) call is copied three times (twice in db.go applyInternal, once in batch.go SyncWait). The reflect.ValueOf(fn).Pointer() check for the no-op callback is fragile.

ROBUSTNESS.evidence: Mutex-guarded heap of waiters on buffered channels; on context cancel it unregisters and re-checks the channel so durability errors win. Limits are named constants (durabilityJobRetention, maxDurabilitySubscriptions). Errors are wrapped with cockroachdb/errors and work with errors.Is. A failure-path test injects a WAL sync error.

C6-03-CASE1.evidence: All new fields and methods are additive. Non-sync commits only gain a crtime.NowMono/Elapsed around apply, with no lock or allocation. Job IDs are allocated only when BatchDurable is configured. NoSyncWait reporting is deferred to SyncWait without new blocking. EnsureDefaults just adds a no-op default for the new hook.
